content: Your physician has prescribed antihemophilic factor (recombinant) to assist your blood in clotting. This medication will be administered either by direct injection into your vein or through an intravenous (IV) fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over a period of approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Depending on your condition, it may be given as frequently as two to three times daily or as infrequently as once every two or more weeks. Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring substance in the body that activates clotting factors in your blood to form clots and reduce bleeding episodes. In some cases, this medication may be used for purposes other than those listed here; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting treatment with antihemophilic factor (recombinant), inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had an allergic reaction to this medication or any other antihemophilic factor. Additionally, disclose any allergies to other drugs. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially aminocaproic acid (Amicar), anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin/Coumadin), corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone), cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), cyclosporine (Neoral, Sandimmune), heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g., Lovenox, Normiflo), interferon alfa (e.g., Roferon-A, Intron), vincristine (Oncovin), vitamin K, and other vitamins. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while using this medication, notify your doctor immediately. If you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your surgeon or dentist that you are taking antihemophilic factor (recombinant). Before administering antihemophilic factor (recombinant), carefully inspect the solution. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not discontinue your treatment without consulting your healthcare provider, and do not alter your dosing schedule without their approval. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume therapy as soon as possible. Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) may cause side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: dizziness, headache, sore throat, itching, upset stomach, vomiting, or fatigue. If you experience any of the following serious symptoms, stop the infusion immediately and contact your healthcare provider: increased heart rate, hives, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, chest discomfort or tightness, chills, or fever. If you experience a severe side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider will likely provide you with a supply of antihemophilic factor (recombinant) for several days at a time and will instruct you on how to prepare each dose. Store the medication as directed by your healthcare provider. Your healthcare provider will also explain how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving antihemophilic factor (recombinant) through a vein or under the skin, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection, which may occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. This medication is available under the brand names Helixate® FS, Kogenate® FS, Recombinate®, and ReFacto®. It is also referred to as AHF or Factor VIII (Recombinant).
